title: Clean foods: illusion or reality?
summary: NH weighs the clean-eating camp against the IIFYM 'a calorie is a calorie' camp. He argues the real difference between foods lies in micronutrients, not macros or calories, while warning that obsessing over clean versus dirty breeds shame and eating disorders; eat whole foods that agree with you and keep diet out of your identity.
claims: Diet is even more case-by-case than training; you must learn your ancestry and what works for you before applying any plan
Dietary needs can change abruptly: a food that worked for a decade can suddenly stop agreeing with you
Diet advice tends to be either uselessly generic or overly precise secret-hack content; both are dangerous
Protein requirements pushed online are usually overshot; missing 10 g of protein a day will not stop your gains
Novices do not need much protein because they have not built the anabolic capacity to use it; the extra just becomes expensive calories better replaced with carbs
Supplement sellers push absurd intakes like 200 g of protein a day for a 112 lb person so you finish the tub faster
Diet has low impact on building muscle once you know what works for you and have balanced macros; training is what really matters
Anyone claiming muscle is 80% diet misunderstands the relation or is on steroids, for whom it is 20% training because drugs do the work
To judge clean foods, ignore calories and macros and look at micronutrients
You can lose weight on a junk food diet because fat loss only requires a caloric deficit, but that misses the point
Potatoes and chocolate cake look similar by macros and calories, but potatoes bring vitamins and minerals and the cake almost none
Most people easily reach maintenance calories, which is all you need for gains, and easily find protein and fat; hitting vitamins and minerals is the hard part on a junk diet
The more junk food you eat, the more the rest of the diet must make up for missing micronutrients; only very hard gainers with high TDEE benefit from junk food
Eating nutrient-rich whole foods to cover micronutrients usually meets caloric needs too
Obsessing over whether everything is clean breeds guilt and shame and can develop into a full eating disorder
Judge foods by whether they agree with you rather than by mainstream clean or dirty labels
No food is clean for everyone: broccoli destroys his stomach, so he does not eat it
Clean foods are interchangeable; you can swap a hated food like chicken for another with similar macros
Same with exercises: if bench hurts your shoulder, dips or weighted push-ups can build the chest
The cultish clean-eating crowd provoked an opposite cult claiming junk food does not exist and pizza equals steamed potatoes, which may be more dangerous
Diet is simple: get enough macros and micros from whole foods, then just maintain the habit
Diet is a tool for health and performance, not a personality trait
